episodes.212363: Thunderstorms, a few which were severe, track north-northeast across the plains of northeast Colorado. Hail up to 1.5 inch in diameter, wind gusts to 70 mph and a tornado.
episodes.212524: Storms moved northeast bringing strong winds to Phillips and Valley counties, respectively.
episodes.212589: Between May 28 and June 4, 2026, a very slow-moving upper-level low-pressure system  over Montana tapped into moisture from the Gulf of America, bringing heavy and widespread precipitation to western Montana. Prior to this event, several locations had already received significant moisture in May, leaving soils saturated and mountain runoff elevated. The combination of intense rainfall and ongoing snowmelt led to swollen rivers, and overwhelmed small streams, and flooded local irrigation canals. Intense thunderstorms brought heavy rain-rates in Sanders County resulting in mudslides.
episodes.212618: Despite dense cloud cover throughout the day, a couple of thunderstorms managed to develop during the evening of the 29th in the southeastern Permian Basin and Lower Trans-Pecos. Heavy rainfall and some thunderstorm training resulted in flash flooding along I-10 and the nearby frontage roads near Bakersfield.
episodes.212679: A strong dryline mixed eastward on the afternoon of the 30th to roughly the Texas Highway 70 corridor. Convergence along the dryline was sufficient for an isolated storm to develop over Motley County. This storm intensified as it moved eastward into Cottle County producing quarter size hail in rural Cottle County.
episodes.212863: A few isolated, strong thunderstorms were observed. No verification was received, but one storm had quarter-sized hail report prior to a warning being issued.
episodes.212865: Several slow-moving thunderstorms developed across the southern Nebraska Panhandle and northern Nebraska Panhandle, bringing hail, tornadoes, and torrential rain fall with flooding occuring in Kimball and Dawes Counties. No verification occurred in southeast Wyoming.
episodes.212969: Strong to severe thunderstorms initiated over far southwestern Nebraska and the Nebraska Panhandle during the late afternoon hours of May 30th. As this activity progressed slowly east into the evening hours, numerous large hail and damaging wind gusts were reported. A couple of tornadoes were also reported. Hail up to 3.5 inches in diameter and thunderstorm wind gusts up to 72 MPH were reported.
episodes.213026: A frontal boundary stalled over southeast Georgia on May 29th and gradually dissipated through May 31st as it meandered southward to the Florida-Georgia border. Deep moisture (PWATs 2+ inches) combined with the frontal boundary and passing shortwaves aloft continued a numerous to widespread shower and thunderstorm pattern each day. Light southwesterly flow ahead of the boundary resulted in slow moving downpours in a Gulf sea breeze dominant regime. Heaviest rainfall amounts were near the I-95 corridor where the Gulf sea breeze collided with the pinned Atlantic sea breeze.
episodes.213217: A cold front moved through the area Friday the 29th, bringing scattered showers during the afternoon and evening as it tracked south across the region. Even with limited instability, strong shear supported a few thunderstorms, mainly across the Mohawk Valley and Tug Hill Plateau. The tightening pressure gradient along and behind the front also produced widespread gusty winds of 30-40 mph, especially across the higher elevations.
episodes.213318: On the evening of May 27th into the morning of the 28th, plenty of atmospheric moisture and lift led to training thunderstorms across the northeastern combined Panhandles. Some flooding eventually occurred in northern Lipscomb County due to the heavy and repeated rainfall. Going into the 29th, moisture and lift continued to lead to thunderstorms, some of which became severe with hail up to golf ball size and wind gusts up to 75 to 80 mph. On the 29th, storms were mainly across the southern TX Panhandle.
episodes.213323: A weak cold front tracked across Eastern North Carolina during the morning and afternoon hours of May thirtieth. As the front tracked across the coastal waters of Eastern North Carolina, scattered showers and thunderstorms developed along the coast with an isolated storm or two becoming strong in nature. The strongest storm that developed produced a waterspout in the Core Sound given the favorable environment.
episodes.213378: Weak ascent atop a very hot/unstable boundary layer fostered clusters of thunderstorms - generally disorganized/multi-cell in nature - from southwestern into north-central Oklahoma on the 29th. Damaging wind gusts and hail were observed with activity throughout the evening.
episodes.213380: A midlevel trough lifting northeast from Arkansas and Mississippi, interacted with a cold front moving in from the north, to cause widespread showers and thunderstorms across East Tennessee from late in the evening on May 29th, through the late morning hours on May 30th. This led to scattered reports of flash flooding across East Tennessee, most notably in the central Tennessee valley and northern Cumberland Plateau areas.
episodes.213409: A couple isolated severe storms produced up to 60-mph wind gusts in Kingman and Rice Counties the night of May 29. No damage was reported from these storms.
episodes.213410: Numerous rounds of strong to severe storms impacted much of the forecast area during the afternoon, evening, and nighttime hours of May 30th. First, a cluster of storms developed across the Flint Hills and progressed eastward across southeast Kansas. These storms produced hail up to half-dollar size and wind gusts estimated to be at least 70 mph. Then, another round of storms developed across portions of south-central and central Kansas producing hail up to ping pong ball size and wind gusts of at least 70 mph. Additionally, a heat burst occurred across portions of central Kansas as storms began dissipating during the nighttime hours, and Salina Regional Airport recorded a non-thunderstorm wind gust of up to 62 mph from the heat burst.
episodes.213452: Thunderstorms developed along an instability axis across central Kansas during the evening hours of May 29 before pushing east towards the Missouri Ozarks in the morning on May 30. This scattered morning activity remained sub-severe, however additional thunderstorm development occurred in the afternoon and evening hours, leading to several reports of damaging winds uprooting trees, extensive damage to a barn, and hail up to the size of quarters. Additional thunderstorms developed over Kansas during the late evening hours, pushing into central Missouri on May 31 and causing thunderstorm wind damage across Pulaski and Dent counties in the early afternoon.
episodes.213525: A sharpening High Plains dryline, in concert with a strong upper level disturbance approaching from the southwest, spawned scattered thunderstorms across western to northwest Kansas during the late afternoon and evening hours on the 30th. Storms moved north to northeast. A measured wind gust to 68 mph and half-dollar sized hail both occurred in Norton County. Additionally, portions of Graham County received dime to nickel sized hail.
episodes.213526: A sharpening High Plains dryline in concert with a strong upper level disturbance approaching from the southwest spawned scattered thunderstorms across northeast Colorado during the late afternoon and evening hours on the 30th. Thunderstorms moved north to slightly northwest. Hail up to ping-pong ball size was measured in Yuma County.  A tornado was reported north of Eckley, but caused no damage.  Further south winds from thunderstorms to the west of Yuma County caused a dust storm southwest of Vernon toward the state line.
episodes.213527: A sharpening High Plains dryline in concert with a strong upper level disturbance approaching from the southwest spawned scattered thunderstorms across southwest Nebraska during the early evening hours on the 30th. Storms moved to the north to slightly northwest. A measured wind gust of 58 mph and quarter sized hail both occurred in Red Willow County.
episodes.213667: A closed low in the area brought two rounds of isolated strong to severe thunderstorms to the region. The main hazard with storms was severe wind gusts.
episodes.213838: Isolated to scattered strong storms developed mainly near and east of the I-65 corridor in the afternoon and early evening hours. A storm knocked down a tree in southern portions of Morgan county.
episodes.214092: Severe storms produced large hail across the Ogalala Lakota area.
episodes.214231: Scattered thunderstorms impacted the southeast Georgia coast in the early evening hours. One storm became strong enough to produce damaging wind gusts in the Savannah area.
episodes.214278: An approaching frontal boundary to the Natural State at the beginning of the episode would become a stationary boundary as the upper level flow pattern would begin as an approaching positively-tilted trough axis which would become an omega block and lock the mesoscale feature of the stationary boundary in position across Arkansas leading to a multiple day period of severe weather.
episodes.214392: A couple of severe thunderstorms occurred.
episodes.214482: A cluster of thunderstorms developed across the North Carolina Piedmont during the morning in advance of a cold front. The relative slow movement of the cluster resulted in heavy-to-torrential rainfall that continued for a couple of hours along the Mecklenburg/Union County line, with flash flooding developing across northern Union County.

events.narrative: A storm chaser reported a few quarter-sized hail stones occurring around 6PM on May 29th. No other reports were received.

Widespread small stream, agricultural, and infrastructural flooding occurred across the Mission Valley due to accelerated snowmelt and 4 to 6 inches of rainfall over a four-day period. A private weather station located 3 miles east-northeast of Pablo measured a total of 5.09 inches of rain from Friday through Monday, while another station just north of the Mission Reservoir measured 3.46 inches. Initial minor flooding began on Friday evening, May 29, when a storm dropped 0.50 to 0.60 inches of rain along the eastern side of the valley, flooding one-third of a private property near St. Ignatius. Runoff rapidly filled local irrigation systems, causing widespread issues.  |At 0600MST on May 31, the lower cylinder flood gate at Mission Dam failed during a high-flow period. While flows were already elevated, this mechanical failure induced a dynamic flow condition where discharges dropped momentarily until emergency teams opened the upper cylinder gate to stabilize the dam, returning outflow into Mission Creek to approximately 350 CFS. At 1000MST, Agency Creek breached its banks, flooding low-lying pastures between Jocko and Agency Roads. At 1300MST, North Crow Creek overflowed, inundating properties along Minesinger Trail. |At 1430MST, the Pablo Feeder Canal experienced a structural failure at Skyline Drive and Caffrey Road, flooding adjacent crop fields. A multi-agency emergency response deployed heavy equipment and placed over 500 sandbags to reinforce the canal's south wall and repair the road base. |On June 1, NWS storm surveys documented extensive field flooding along Red Horn, Hillside, and Foothills Roads due to out-of-bank tributaries. North Crow Creek completely left its banks around Timberlane Road, inundating driveways and spreading water within 1 to 2 feet of a home's foundation. Floodwaters along the Pablo Feeder Canal completely submerged a length of Minesinger Trail and Mountain View Road, rendering them impassable to traffic. At 1400MST on June 1, with the Kicking Horse Reservoir at full capacity, all active water diversions from South Crow into the reservoir ceased. This forced the unbuffered, full natural flow from the South Crow drainage directly downstream into Crow Creek. The resulting surge caused Crow Creek to leave its banks entirely, backing up directly into a commercial greenhouse business (Bev's Bloomers). The floodwaters came within one foot of an adjacent home's foundation, and left a 6-foot property fence completely underwater. Severe road washouts were also reported north of Arlee on Saddle Mountain Road, where heavy rains stripped away soil and gravel to expose bedrock. Debris, mud, and water gushed across Highway MT-35 at milepost 10 on Monday evening, carrying a boulder the size of a small car onto the driving lanes near Woods Bay.

A training thunderstorm positioned over the Eddy basin dropped between 1.41 and 1.60 inches of rain in less than 1.5 hours. This high-intensity rainfall fell on steep terrain, rapidly saturating soils and triggering multiple mudslides on the mountainside north of Highway 200. The resulting debris flow rushed down the slope 2 miles east-southeast of Eddy, uprooting at least one large tree and dislodging a boulder the size of a small car. The massive boulder and associated mud slide debris slid directly into the roadway, completely blocking traffic between mile markers 63 and 64. The local fire department and state road crews responded to manage traffic and clear the slide area.

Emergency manager and public reported flash flooding developed in the Crooked Creek basin after 2 to 3.5 inches of rain fell along the Mecklenburg/Union County line in just a couple of hours. This was on the heels of a string of days that saw scattered afternoon thunderstorms bring heavy rainfall to the area. Flooding of a parking lot adjacent to the intersection of Indian Trail Fairview Rd and Idlewild Rd was reported and a small portion of Indian Trail Fairview Rd was closed as a result. The lower level of a home flooded near the intersection of White Oak Ln and Cupped Oak Dr, as did the intersection itself. Other roads reported to have flooded included Lawyers Rd at N Rocky River Rd and Oak Spring Rd.
Several roads impacted by flooding across Loudon County, including Highway 72, Vonore Road, Meadow Road West near Big Hill Road, Highland Avenue, ,and Old Highway 95.

Although heavy rainfall tapered off across northern Union County during late morning, high water conditions continued across mainly the Crooked Creek basin as runoff from the earlier rainfall continued to result in elevated stream levels and flows.
